title: Huh.
description:
## What.
Now, you may have noticed that the syntax looks like a blobfish when outside of water. That is correct. Haskell is something called a _Functional Programming Language_, which basically means that you describe what you want to happen instead of how it should happen. First, before we get into Haskell monstrosities, let's cover the boilerplate.
Haskell programs start in main:
```haskell
main :: IO ()
```
This basically means "main is an action that can perform input/output and returns no useful value.", to break this down: `main`: this is called main. `::`: think of this as saying "has type", so main has type IO (). `IO`: This means the function can perform input/output, like printing or reading input. `()`: This function returns nothing meaningful.
Now, actually printing to console. To actually code in a function, there is a simple rule: For single line, you can just do this:
```haskell
main = <code>
```
However, if you have multiple lines, you must do
```haskell
main = do
    <code>
```
A `do` block lets you write multiple actions in sequence, using indentation to group them. To print a string you use `putStrLn "text here"`.
You may be seeing all this function talk. Don't worry, they're coming soon.

---
## Assignment:
Somebody deleted our main function! Recreate it. It should welcome our users to their new phone. Make it print 2 lines, `Welcome to your new pPhone 18!`, and `Bonus screen protectors available for 299.99`.
expectedOutput:
Welcome to your new pPhone 18!
Bonus screen protectors available for 299.99
